title: The vertex set of a 0/1-polytope is strongly P-enumerable
contribution: Proves that the vertices of every polytope whose vertices lie among those of a known combinatorial cube, in particular of every 0/1-polytope, can be listed in time linear in the output and space independent of it, by a binary partition tree with one feasibility LP per node, derives a max-flow enumeration of all 0/1 flows, and releases the CPLEX-based code zerone.
problem_entry: An open complexity question (is vertex enumeration polynomial in input and output size?), entered through strong P-enumerability and a class on which backtracking needs NP-complete node decisions, Provan's method is quadratic in the output and reverse search needs simple polytopes (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: If all vertices lie among those of a squashed cube with known facet pairs, each vertex is one facet choice per pair; build the choices in a binary tree and prune by an LP feasibility check, which a hereditary property makes exact; the unit cube makes the extra input free for 0/1-polytopes; replace the LP by max flow to enumerate 0/1 flows directly (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Class of convex hulls of vertex subsets of a full-dimensional polytope combinatorially equivalent to the cube, whose description must be supplied as redundant input (free for 0/1-polytopes); the result explicitly says nothing about enumerating combinatorial objects such as Hamiltonian cycles; no instance library (pp. 3-5).
proof_devices: Theorem 2, correctness by a hereditary property: P intersected with a facet of the cube stays in the class, so one LP decides whether a vertex lies below a node, and each leaf of the binary partition tree is reached once (pp. 4-5)
Theorem 3, complexity O(v n T_FP) with at most n LPs per output vertex and O((m+n)n) space (p. 5)
Redundant input: the cube's description is added to P's so that the algorithm can rely on it (p. 4)
Corollaries 4-5: strong P-enumerability for the class and, with the unit cube as boundary, for all 0/1-polytopes (p. 5)
Algorithm 2 and Corollary 6: 0/1-flow enumeration with O(m) max-flow existence tests per output, correctness inherited from Theorem 2 (pp. 6-7)
Counterexample remark: the polar of a polytope in the class need not be in the class, checked in dimension three (p. 8)
experiments: Two timings on an HP9000/735-125 (the 20-dimensional unit cube in under twenty minutes; the 5,040 vertices of a bipartite matching polytope on two times seven nodes in about eight minutes); comparison with double description or reverse search declined as unfair; the benefit claimed is output-independent memory (p. 6).
positioning: Builds on Valiant and on Fukuda, Liebling and Margot; generalizes Fukuda and Matsui and a result of his own 1996 Master's thesis (ref. [7]); contrasts with double description and reverse search without measuring them; names Bremner, Fukuda and Marzetta for facet enumeration (pp. 2-3, 5, 6, 8).
writing: Definitions, two theorems with short proofs and three corollaries, then a conclusions-and-open-problems section whose hedges sit where the result stops ('not known to the authors', a labelled conjecture); the abstract's 'superior to general vertex enumeration algorithms' outruns a body that declines every comparison (pp. 1, 6, 7-8).
limits_future: Depends on a cube description the authors cannot construct efficiently; no immediate generalization; backtracking conjectured not to give more general results; facet enumeration open, the polar no help; future: combine with Bremner, Fukuda and Marzetta to list the facets of the class (pp. 7-8).

method_links.note: Enumeration as the object of a theorem rather than a map of design options; the bridge is the named use, listing all integral vertices of a model's polytope even when nothing is known about its 0/1-property, an instrument for checking integrality by computation [inferred link to letting computation suggest the theorem]
Exit B in its theory form: proved for one class (0/1-polytopes and the cube-hull class), the general case published as an open question and a conjecture

Step 6 for the theoretical claim: the scope of the result fenced by an explicit input-size caveat with the Hamiltonian-cycle counterexample. Also Taste G2 (code released, p. 6) and Taste G4 (Algorithm 2 works directly on the problem rather than on the polytope, p. 6)
Step 6 for the computational claim (co-signed, 1998): 'superior' in the abstract rests only on Theorem 3's memory bound and two timings, while the body declines a comparison as unfair

transferable: Correctness by a hereditary property: show that every face the recursion enters stays in the class, so that one LP or one combinatorial existence test per node decides whether an output lies below it (pp. 4-5)
Bound the LPs per output by the recursion depth to get time linear in the output and memory independent of it (p. 5)
Take a structure you cannot compute as redundant input, prove the result conditional on it, and name the case where it is free (the unit cube for 0/1-polytopes) (pp. 4-5)
Specialize a polyhedral enumeration to a combinatorial one by swapping the LP feasibility test for a max-flow existence test (pp. 6-7)
Before trying to prove a formulation integral, enumerate the vertices of its polytope on small instances (p. 6)
Open a complexity note by placing your class between the general open question and the settled special cases, each with the reason the known method fails on it (p. 3)
coauthors: Michael R. Bussieck (first author); Lübbecke second and corresponding author; both TU Braunschweig, Department of Mathematical Optimization

quotes.text: We prefer not to give comparative computational results because a comparison with more general algorithms such as the double description method or the reverse search technique is obviously unfair.
We emphasize that these statements do not measure the complexity of combinatorial optimization or enumeration problems

title: Engine routing and scheduling at industrial in-plant railroads
contribution: Models in-plant railroad engine scheduling, a pickup and delivery problem with time windows restricted to railroad-mandated schedule patterns, as a MIP and as its set-partitioning Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation, solves the LP by column generation with a new exact label-correcting pricing algorithm pruned by dual-variable-based bounds inside a heuristic pricing cascade, and obtains integer plans by price-and-branch on real and artificial data.
problem_entry: Engines dispatched first-come, first-served by pencil and paper under truck competition, with almost no OR literature; posed as a multiple-vehicle pickup and delivery problem with time windows plus the patterns yard managers insist on, 'part of the problem, not its simplification' (pp. 1-2). Workflow A and Heuristic H3: owner-set restrictions, officer-approved data, horizon and objective set by the railroad (pp. 2, 10, 12, 13).
key_idea: ESPMIP written for insight and ESPSP as its Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation; column generation with elementary constrained shortest path pricing on a pattern graph, solved by a label-correcting DP with dual-bound pruning, heuristics and a pool, exact pricing only to prove LP optimality; price-and-branch (columns at the root only) for integer solutions (pp. 3-10).
assumptions: Requests with tracks, loads, service times and time windows; heterogeneous engines with tractive efforts; a two-hour horizon; strongly NP-complete even for feasibility, pricing strongly NP-complete; objective deadheading plus waiting time; data vps (a real shift, officer-approved modifications), eko820 (a real log with generated windows and estimated distances, 'cannot be regarded as real-life data'), eko80x (generated hard) and Sol's random m-PDPTW classes used as raw data; integer costs with rounding of 1e-15 deviations (pp. 2-5, 9-11).
proof_devices: Strong NP-completeness of the scheduling problem by reduction from the multiple TSP with time windows, even for feasibility (p. 3), and of the pricing problem by reduction from LONGEST PATH (p. 5)
Formal derivation of the set-partitioning model as the Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation of the MIP, the subproblem solved by DP because its LP bound is poor (p. 4)
Label-correcting DP on the pattern graph: states (R, i), two-dimensional nondominated labels, chronological order with a time-window break (pp. 5-6)

Dual-variable-based label elimination: LB_R = cheapest label at state R minus the positive duals of admissible requests not in R; prune when LB_R >= min{0, C_inc}, optimality preserved (eqs. 15-16, pp. 6-7)

Pricing cascade: column pool, greedy dual-per-slack heuristic, exact DP stopped at the 100th negative column, full exact pricing only to prove LP optimality; cyclic per-engine pricing with RMP re-optimization (pp. 9-11)
Pool anti-cycling rule: positive-reduced-cost pool columns only together with a negative one (p. 9)
Cost-coefficient improvement by backtracking for request sets with |R| <= 4 (pp. 7-8)
Price-and-branch: column generation at the root only, then branch-and-bound on the generated columns (pp. 8-9)
Numerical safeguard: dual-based values off by about 1e-15 rounded to the nearest integer (p. 11)
experiments: Pentium III 700 MHz, CPLEX 7.0; vps10-vps39, eko820a-c in groups of 25, eko80x and Sol's A, B, C, D and DAR classes; LP value, integer value, gap, B&B and total time, columns, simplex iterations, engines used; ablation of the label-elimination criterion with a one-CPU-week cap (vps36-vps39 exceed it without; vps35 58.45 s against 501,309.84 s, read as two-decimal values); failures printed (wide windows, short distances, unsolved eko80x rows, class D); the Sol comparison flagged as a different objective and horizon; no comparison with practice possible (pp. 7, 10-14).
positioning: m-PDPTW literature (Savelsbergh and Sol, Dumas et al., Sol) and mostly Montréal column generation and labelling (Desaulniers et al., Desrochers and Soumis, Desrosiers et al., Gegen et al.); recommends the Desaulniers, Desrosiers and Solomon acceleration review before any implementation; Desrosiers read the drafts (Heuristic H10); no competitor criticized (pp. 2-6, 9, 15).
writing: Abstract: 'All the claims are demonstrated'; experience statements in the implementation section; specific hedges ('Admittedly'; not 'a mathematically satisfactory explanation'); a Remarks section of limits rather than a summary; one overreach, 'always obtaining (even optimal) integer solutions', beside unsolved rows of Table 4; proofs deferred to the thesis (pp. 1, 9, 11, 13).
limits_future: No comparison with practice; exact pricing is the bottleneck; needs a small pattern family; label data structures and network reduction not studied; everyday computability still to be established; no branch-and-price safeguard; future: stochastic engine availability and requests, the online version (pp. 9, 13).

method_links.note: Steps 1 and 3: the compact MIP is written first for insight and the extended model derived from it by Dantzig-Wolfe; pattern concatenations become variables because their pricing is solvable by DP while the subproblem's LP bound is poor. Step 5 context: no branch-and-price, named 'additional effort' and justified by observed integrality, with branch-and-price as the industrial safeguard (fits the podcast reason). Also Heuristic H1 (strong, 2002-2003 practice): exact pricing only for the certificate, several columns per round, pool, greedy and truncated exact DP before a full exact call, cyclic partial pricing
Step 2: the compact MIP is never run in a solver; the computational section has no compact baseline, so the decomposition is not measured against it

One-component ablation of the label-elimination criterion on the same machine under a stated cap; failures and limits printed; data provenance and synthetic parts declared; the comparison with Sol's optima flagged as a different objective and horizon

Step 6: 'always obtaining (even optimal) integer solutions' beside unsolved rows of Table 4, and 'All the claims are demonstrated' in the abstract; no seed protocol, consistent with the skill's stated limitation

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A branch-and-bound lower-bound test transplanted into the pricing DP: a bound from the duals not yet collected prunes states, on the stated similarity of DP and branch-and-bound as implicit enumeration; from his 1999 report; check S033 (EJOR 2005) before pooling

transferable: Dual-bound pruning in a labelling pricing algorithm: LB_R = cheapest label at state R minus the positive duals of admissible requests outside R; drop the state when LB_R >= min{0, incumbent} (pp. 6-7)

Pricing cascade: column pool, then a greedy dual-per-slack heuristic, then the exact DP stopped at the k-th negative column (k = 100), and the full exact DP only when every engine fails, to prove LP optimality (pp. 9-11)
Pool anti-cycling rule: add pool columns of small positive reduced cost only in an iteration that also adds a negative one (p. 9)
Cyclic partial pricing over blocks with an RMP re-optimization after each block, so that later blocks price with fresh duals (p. 10)
Ablate one algorithmic component by rerunning the whole table without it under a stated time cap, and print the cap (p. 7)
Declare data provenance: which instances are real, which parts were modified and who approved them, which parts are synthetic (pp. 10-11)
Write practitioner-imposed solution shapes into the problem definition as a finite pattern set and say why it is not a relaxation device (p. 2)
When your instances relax a literature benchmark, state the difference next to the comparison and explain any result that beats the published optimum (pp. 12-13)
coauthors: Uwe T. Zimmermann (doctoral advisor); Lübbecke first author; TU Braunschweig; Jacques Desrosiers thanked for reading drafts

quotes.text: it is neither mandatory to add a most profitable column to the restricted master program, nor are we restricted to adding only one column at a time
We avoided the additional effort of implementing a branch-and-price algorithm. This is well justified by our always obtaining (even optimal) integer solutions.

title: A fast algorithm for near cost optimal line plans
contribution: For cost-optimal line planning at the Dutch Railways, combines a nonconvex MINLP with two new integer linearizations and problem-specific valid inequalities into FIX, a heuristic in which the MINLP relaxation fixes unpromising routes in the ILP, an incumbent is found within minutes and the fixing is released for exact branch-and-bound; best feasible solutions on three of four instances in about five minutes, code public.
problem_entry: Exact work gave strong lower bounds but no matching primal solutions and earlier heuristics failed; a methodological aim to integrate MINLP and MIP by reviving a dropped MINLP model; practitioners need good solutions fast (pp. 2-3, 8).
key_idea: Each model does what it is good at: the continuous MINLP relaxation, started from an ILP's LP point, only decides which routes to fix to zero in the ILP; the restricted ILP gives an incumbent; then the fixing is dropped, cuts added and exact branch-and-bound continues from a warm start, 'a very careful initialization of branch-and-bound' (pp. 9-10).
assumptions: Rail network with predefined routes, small integer frequency sets including zero, per-edge frequency bounds and coach demand, a single coach type, fixed and per-kilometre costs; strongly NP-hard; bilinear and ceiling terms; the MINLP simplification exact for hourly frequencies and within 3% average error on the solutions found; four Dutch Railways instances ic97, ic98, ir98, ar98 that had circulated for years (pp. 3-6, 9).
proof_devices: Simplification of the trains-needed ceiling term, exact for hourly frequencies (p. 5)
Three linearizations BLP, ILP and ILP-C; ILP-C reduces to BLP with fixed frequency when only one nonzero frequency is allowed (pp. 5-7)
Propositions 1-4: valid inequalities argued from the problem, carrying over to all linearizations, proofs deferred to Bussieck's thesis (pp. 7-8)
Separation restricted to polynomial subfamilies at the root only (cut-and-branch), giving model CUT (p. 8)
Algorithm 1 FIX: LP of ILP, NLP initialization, continuous NLP, fixing at threshold 1e-5, fixed ILP, fixings dropped, cuts added and non-binding ones removed, warm start, branch-and-bound (p. 10)
experiments: GAMS 20.6, CONOPT2 and SBB, CPLEX 7.5, 700 MHz Linux PC, three hours; four instances; baselines standard branch-and-bound on BLP and ILP for the full limit, optima from CUT (ic97 by Bixby in a month); a qualitative comparison in bound-over-time figures; counts given (FIX best on three of four in about five minutes; ir98 the exception); Table 1 cut counts and LP gains; Table 2 guidance ablation, the NLP's benefit 'marginal'; Goossens et al. not compared (different data); single runs (pp. 9-11, 13-14).
positioning: The cost side of line planning; continues Bussieck's thesis and Claessens et al.; credits Goossens et al. (lower bounds) and Fischetti and Lodi (feasibility); the MINLP software landscape and an OR/MS Today call for more nonlinear optimization; earlier heuristics judged as failing; a pro-MINLP stance, a variant of the skill's Taste G5 and its Weak-at line on nonlinear optimization (pp. 2-3, 8-9, 11-12).
writing: Strong framing ('a new and surprising development'; 'this—and only this—is relevant to practitioners'), measured results ('Admittedly'; 'serious comparisons cannot be drawn'), a reflective conclusion on solver progress and on what counts as 'a practical algorithm', and a field-level reproducibility statement (pp. 3, 9, 11-12).
limits_future: FIX is a heuristic; the NLP adds little; four instances and a qualitative comparison; usefulness tied to commercial solver progress (future CPLEX versions may make it obsolete); future: lines not run back and forth, robustness for timetabling, non-dedicated rolling stock, column generation for the cost version, integrated planning (pp. 9-12).

method_links.note: The yardstick logic outside decomposition (steps 2 and 5): plain branch-and-bound on BLP and ILP for the full limit is the baseline; the algorithm initializes the solver's own tree; an off-the-shelf product is often much superior to tailored algorithms

The exception instance reported in full, the poor ILP-C stated, a non-comparable literature result flagged, the guidance benefit called marginal, counts given; solver dependence stated after experiments with CPLEX 2.0 through 8.0 (Workflow F step 3). Also Taste G2 (code public so readers can check claims, p. 9) and Taste G1 with Heuristic H2 (heuristic solutions judged against linearization bounds, pp. 2, 10)
Four instances, single runs, the main comparison only in figures; the introduction's 'new and surprising development' is larger than the ablation's 'marginal'

Step 1: the option space of model combinations is written down and measured (four combinations), but the NLP is kept because it most naturally reflects the practical background, a choice by modelling taste after the measurement showed little gain

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The relaxation of one model (a nonconvex MINLP) fixes variables of another (the ILP) for an incumbent, then the fixing is released for exact search; check later works (e.g. S042) before pooling

transferable: FIX: relax the nonconvex MINLP from the linearization's LP point, fix to zero the variables of routes the relaxation sends to zero (threshold 1e-5), solve the restricted ILP for an incumbent, then drop the fixings and run exact branch-and-bound with cuts from a warm start (pp. 9-10)

For a product of two integer variables, compare three linearizations (binaries per value combination; binary plus integer by frequency; binary plus integer by capacity) and keep the one whose structure survives the other modelling needs, such as domain holes and ceiling terms (pp. 5-7)
Present valid inequalities through the problem argument, separate only polynomial subfamilies and only at the root, and report per-class violated counts with the LP gain in one table (pp. 7-8, 11)
Baseline protocol for a primal heuristic on a hard MIP: run the plain models in the solver for the whole limit and plot primal and dual bounds over time next to the heuristic (pp. 10, 13-14)
Ablate the guidance step of a multi-model heuristic at a fixed short time (guided against unguided, two base models) and print it even when the guidance barely helps (p. 11)
State the solver versions a method was tested against and the condition under which a future solver would make it obsolete (pp. 11-12)
Release code with the reason given: readers must be able to check claims the paper's numbers do not cover (p. 9)
coauthors: Michael R. Bussieck (first author, GAMS Development Corporation), Thomas Lindner (Siemens Transportation Systems); Lübbecke third, TU Berlin

quotes.text: In contrast, we would like to enable the reader to check claims which we do not explicitly support by numerical results.
Not seldom we see that we can learn a lot from a tailored algorithm but an off-the-shelf product is much superior in terms of computation time, and often quality.

title: Selected topics in column generation
contribution: Survey, read in its March 2004 preprint, that unifies Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition, Lagrangian relaxation and integer column generation in one notation and reads the restricted master, pricing, tailing off, stabilization and branching through the dual point of view, recommending compact formulations and branching and cutting on their original variables.
problem_entry: A literature gap: integer column generation is a success and recent contributions are not yet in textbooks; biased toward integer programs; opens by correcting the misconception that integrality can simply be imposed on the generated variables (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: The dual point of view organizes the field: the RMP provides duals, pricing is dual separation (Kelley), the Dantzig-Wolfe bound equals the Lagrangian bound, and initialization, dual-optimal inequalities, aggregation and stabilization act on the duals; for integer programs it all boils down to branch-and-bound on the original variables of a compact formulation (pp. 8-9, 13-16, 20-24).
assumptions: Integer programs with X = P intersected with the integer lattice (possibly nonlinear aspects) and a finite optimum; block-diagonal structure; set-partitioning and covering masters; each tool's condition stated (an upper bound on the sum of the master variables for bound (5), c >= 0 for Farley, bounded X for discretization, 0/1 sets where convexification equals discretization, mild assumptions for a compact formulation, integer costs for early termination, a linear subproblem for Walker, a 0/1 matrix for Ryan-Foster; massive degeneracy beyond about ten nonzeros per column); no instance library (pp. 6-8, 11, 16, 22-24).
proof_devices: Iteration bounds: Lagrangian lower bound with the master's column-sum bound, the unit-cost ratio bound, Farley's bound and the block version (pp. 6-8)
Equality of the Dantzig-Wolfe RMP bound and the Lagrangian bound via the LP form of the Lagrangian dual (pp. 8-9)
Theorem 1 (discretization) and the remark that convexification and discretization coincide for 0/1 sets (pp. 10-11)
Counterexample (28): without branching, Dantzig's rule never generates a variable the unique integer optimum needs (p. 12)
Separation-optimization equivalence: RMPs polynomially solvable when pricing is, NP-hard when pricing is (p. 15)
Dual-optimal (structural) inequalities, e.g. ordered cutting-stock duals and their subset version (29) (p. 15)
Proposition 2: a strictly redundant column is never optimal for the ratio pricing rule (31) (p. 17)
Wentges's weighted Dantzig-Wolfe with proved finiteness (pp. 20-21); du Merle et al.'s penalized dual box (34)-(35) with stopping criteria and update rules (pp. 21-22)
Early termination when the rounded-up lower bound equals the rounded-up RMP value, with integer costs (pp. 22-23)
Pricing out original variables (Walker; Poggi de Aragão and Uchoa) (p. 23); Proposition 3, Ryan-Foster branching (p. 24)
experiments: none (survey); relays others' numbers with their sources: a factor of 100 from constraining duals to an interval (Ben Amor), a factor of eight from row aggregation at 1,600 rows (Elhallaoui et al.), up to a factor of ten from stabilization, over 90% of flow variables removed by reduced-cost fixing (Hadjar et al.) (pp. 16, 22-23).
positioning: History from Ford and Fulkerson, Dantzig and Wolfe and Gilmore and Gomory to Desrosiers, Soumis and Desrochers 1984; credits Barnhart et al., Vanderbeck and Wolsey, Desaulniers et al.; weight on Montréal work and on Vanderbeck; judges old ideas (subgradients use local information only, aged pricing rules unassessed, classical Dantzig-Wolfe not recommended for LPs, Chvátal's 1983 pessimism no longer true); attributes the weak cutting-stock formulation to Kantorovich 1960 (pp. 3, 10, 12, 18, 25).
writing: Two parts, theory then algorithms; opinions marked ('In our opinion', 'Our point is'); open points marked as open; the conclusion repeats the abstract's dual-view sentences, then recommends and advises; one status claim for generic codes over commercial MIP solvers without a count or citation (pp. 2-3, 10, 13, 18-19, 22, 25).
limits_future: Open: the theory of tailing off, bundle and analytic-centre methods in integer programming, alternative pricing rules, complementary slackness; stabilization needs problem-specific parameters; the implementation burden comes from tuning; the compact formulation must be represented besides master and pricing; 'ample room for research and experiments is left' (pp. 10, 18-19, 22, 25).

method_links.note: Steps 2, 4 and 5: the explanations and remedies of tailing off and dual oscillation collected in one notation; untested and not-understood points written as such; the aim stated as material not yet in textbooks

Step 1: the text names no own runs as its origin (that rests on the podcast self-report); step 6: the Kantorovich 1960 attribution of the weak formulation stands here, the wording the 2026 book corrects (research note 05 section 6)

Steps 1, 3 and 6 and the Workflow B check: look for a compact formulation; decomposition pays only if repeatedly solving the subproblems is easier; the bound gain without the integrality property weighed against fast combinatorial pricing with it; branch and cut on the original variables; the compact formulation must be represented. Also Heuristic H1: approximate pricing until the last iteration, partial pricing, many columns per DP call, early termination and branching when tailing off occurs
Step 6 in a survey: generic integer column generation codes said to solve many large-scale problems that no standard commercial MIP solver could cope with, without a count or a citation

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Every column generation component read through the duals it produces or consumes: the RMP as dual provider, pricing as dual separation, stabilization and dual-optimal inequalities as dual control; the Primer states the same (S002 p. 15)

transferable: Compute the Lagrangian bound at every column generation iteration (with the master's column-sum bound, or one term per block) and, with integer costs, stop the node once the rounded-up bound equals the rounded-up RMP value, then branch (pp. 6-8, 22-23)
Before column generation starts, add dual-optimal inequalities derived from problem structure (cutting stock: duals ordered like the order widths, and the subset version (29)) (p. 15)
Retrieve the duals of the subproblem constraints from the last pricing LP (Walker) and fix original variables whose reduced cost exceeds the gap (p. 23)
Stabilize with a penalized dual box (34)-(35): if the new dual lies in the box, shrink it and raise the penalty, otherwise enlarge it and lower the penalty, updating at each new best dual (pp. 21-22)
Branch on original variables of a compact formulation, and push the decision into the pricing problem when its algorithm can absorb it (p. 24)
To decide on the subproblem's integrality property, weigh the root gap against the speed of a combinatorial pricing algorithm (p. 18)
In a survey, end each topic with a sentence on what is untested or not understood, so that the list of open questions writes itself (pp. 10, 18, 19)
coauthors: Jacques Desrosiers (HEC Montréal and GERAD); Lübbecke first author, TU Berlin

quotes.text: Some imagination is needed to find an appropriate compact formulation, but we strongly recommend to look for one.
Our most valuable source of information are the original variables of the compact formulation; they must be integer, and they are what we branch and cut on

title: A primer in column generation
contribution: Didactic chapter, read in a pre-publication copy, that carries one six-node resource-constrained shortest path instance through reformulation, column generation, branching on original variables, bounds, reduced-cost arc elimination, a subproblem cut, the Lagrangian dual and stabilization, then uses cutting stock to show that one master has several compact formulations that differ in bound, symmetry and branching.
problem_entry: A teaching problem solved 'right away': a six-node constrained shortest path instance that is almost a shortest path problem, whose embedded structure should be exploited (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: One tiny instance carries every concept with all numbers in tables; the original formulation is the control center for branching and cutting, the master gives duals and bounds, the subproblem carries the structure; the dual side explains convergence and stabilization; the choice of compact formulation matters beyond the bound (pp. 1-26).
assumptions: Integer programs with a subproblem set of nonnegative integer points satisfying Dx >= d, a finite optimum and possibly block-diagonal structure; Villeneuve et al.'s assumptions for a compact formulation (bounded sum of master variables, boundable subproblem domain); the running instance from Ahuja et al. 1993, p. 599, with time limit 14; cutting stock with rolls of width L; no instance library (pp. 1-2, 8, 10, 22-23).
proof_devices: Worked branch-and-price on a six-node RCSP: big-M root, branching on arc-flow sums and single arcs, optimal path 13246 of cost 13 (pp. 4-7)
Big-M pitfall: M = 100 too small blocks column generation; a phase I on the artificial variable would prevent it (p. 5)
Bounds (1.21), (1.31), (1.34) and the non-monotone root lower bound 3.0, -8.33, 6.6, 6.5, 7 (pp. 8, 11-12)
Arc elimination by reduced cost from full duals: arc (3,4) at 11 above the gap of 8 (pp. 12-13)
Lower-bound cut added to the subproblem closes the root gap at 13 at the cost of the network structure (p. 14)
Dual box from -2.1 to -1.9 around a subgradient multiplier: the root LP in three iterations (pp. 19-20)
Lagrangian function as the lower envelope of one line per path, explaining the non-monotone bound and fast stabilized convergence (pp. 20-21)

Cutting stock: Gilmore and Gomory's covering form with simple dual-optimal inequalities, the weak and symmetric Kantorovich-type compact formulation, Valério de Carvalho's arc flow with the integrality property (pp. 22-26)
experiments: none; hand-size tables of the running example (Tables 1.1-1.6), cross-checked by Steffen Rebennack (pp. 4-20, 27).
positioning: Based on S001; leaves implementation to Desaulniers et al. 2001 and decomposition choice and heading-in to Vanderbeck's chapter; credits Valério de Carvalho, Ben Amor and the Montréal stabilization work; Lasdon 1970 'an indispensable source'; history told through Ford and Fulkerson's and Gilmore and Gomory's words; attributes the weak formulation to Kantorovich 1939 (pp. 14, 17-18, 22-27).
writing: A didactic register with imperatives and reader address ('Always remember', 'The reader can verify', 'We encourage the reader'), sections named by purpose, a textbook gap named ('left out in textbooks'); closes with Further Reading and a forecast of off-the-shelf column generation software (pp. 1, 3, 11, 13, 15, 18-19, 22, 26).
limits_future: Implementation issues said to be covered only a little; future: automatic detection of the best decomposition of a given original formulation, exploiting the absence of the subproblem's integrality property (p. 26).

method_links.note: Steps 1, 3 and 6: integrality must hold for the original x variables; the original formulation is the control center for branching and cutting and receives branching constraints before the reformulation is re-applied; customized branching rules read as branching on original variables; the exploited structure is the subproblem's. Also Heuristic H1 (any negative column suffices, pools, partial pricing, premature stops with a dual-based bound, pp. 14-15), Heuristic H5 (one master, several compact formulations differing in bound, symmetry and branching, pp. 22-26) and Workflow B (richer subproblems can raise the bound; a structure-destroying cut only if it pays, pp. 13-14)

The increment: in 2005 the vision is off-the-shelf column generation software for large integer programs, with automatic detection of the best decomposition as a crucial part, the generic-solver goal that the skill says became GCG as a first try and an estimate after 2017; the decomposition choice named here is the one the 2015 and 2017 papers take up by enumeration and learning (Method 2) [inferred]
The didactic companion of the survey, written to fill a textbook gap, its numbers checked by a third person

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one tiny running example through every component, cross-checked
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A six-node instance carries reformulation, branching, bounds, arc elimination, cuts, stabilization and the Lagrangian picture, with a named colleague cross-checking the numbers; check the 2026 book before pooling

The generation process and the stopping criteria are driven entirely by the dual multipliers; the dual view explains the non-monotone bound and the fast stabilized convergence on the example (with S001)

transferable: Test or teach a decomposition on an instance small enough to list all columns by hand, and run every component (branching, cuts, stabilization) on it with all numbers in tables (pp. 1-21)
Phase I by minimizing the artificial variables instead of big-M; with big-M, a too-small M can stop column generation with no negative column although feasible columns exist (p. 5)
At the end of the root, compute the full duals of the subproblem constraints and delete every arc whose reduced cost exceeds the current gap (pp. 12-13)
Add the cut objective >= lower bound (and <= upper bound) to a single-block subproblem when the bound gain pays for the lost structure; try it on a small case first (pp. 12, 14)
Warm the root with a small dual box around a subgradient estimate of the multipliers (pp. 19-20)
Choose among compact formulations of the same master by branching and symmetry, not by bound alone (pp. 24-26)
Draw the Lagrangian function as the lower envelope of one line per column to explain non-monotone bounds and stabilization on a small case (pp. 20-21)
In a tutorial, name the step that textbooks leave out and work it through on the running example (p. 18)
